questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 62-year-old man presents to the casualty with a severe headache, fever, and vomiting for the past 8 hours. His CT scan and CSF appearance are shown below. The affected vessels do not get a contribution from:
questions.explanation:
These patient's clinical features as well as the CT scan showing blood in the cistern and the
xanthochromatic CSF appearance are suggestive of subarachnoid haemorrhage. The affected
vessels i.e. the circle of Willis do not get a contribution from the middle cerebral artery.
The circle of Willis is located in the interpeduncular fossa at the base of the brain. It is an
anastomosis between the internal carotid arteries and vertebral arteries. It allows the blood
entering from either artery to be distributed to both the cerebral hemispheres.
The arteries forming the circle of Willis are:
+ Anterior communicating artery
+ Anterior cerebral arteries
+ Internal carotid arteries
+ Posterior communicating arteries

+ Posterior cerebral arteries
+ Basilar artery

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The chief artery of the superolateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere is:
questions.explanation:
The chief artery of the superolateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere is the middle cerebral
artery.
Both the anterior and middle cerebral artery supply the superolateral surface of the brain but
anterior cerebral artery supplies only a narrow strip at the upper superolateral surface rest is
supplied by the middle cerebral artery. Therefore, the chief artery is the middle cerebral artery.
The chief artery of the medial surface of the brain is an anterior cerebral artery.
The chief artery of the inferior surface of the brain is the posterior cerebral artery”
Lateral cerebral artery is not an artery. ae e.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient presents with vertigo, nystagmus, left-sided Horner's syndrome with numbness of left face and right limbs. What is the largest branch of the affected artery marked in the image as 'X'?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Wallenberg's syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome)
and the marked vessel is the vertebral artery. The largest branch of this artery is the posterior
inferior cerebellar artery.
The vertebral artery is a branch of the first part of the subclavian artery. It enters the skull
through the foramen magnum and terminates by joining the vertebral artery of the opposite side
forming the basilar artery. The branches of the cranial portion of the vertebral artery are:
+ Meningeal branches - supplying dura of posterior cranial fossa
+ Posterior spinal arteries - supply posterior one-third of the spinal cord
+ Anterior spinal artery - supply anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord
+ Posterior inferior cerebellar artery - supplies the lateral part of the medulla, cerebellar
hemisphere, and the choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle.
+ Medullary branches - supplying the medulla
The image given below shows the vertebral artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: What structure receives drainage from the superficial middle cerebral vein?
questions.explanation:
The superficial middle cerebral vein drains into the cavernous sinus.
Superficial middle cerebral vein lies in the lateral sulcus and drains most of the lateral surface of
the hemispheres. It drains into the cavernous sinus.

Superficial middle cerebral vein is connected to the superior sagittal sinus through the superior
anastomotic vein of Trolord and to the transverse sinus through the inferior anastomotic vein of
Labbe.
